claimed.text: Graves testified in writing that his squadron began witnessing advanced UAP demonstrating complex manoeuvres on a regular basis after the AESA radar upgrade, and told 60 Minutes the sightings came every day for at least a couple of years.

In Graves's account, the pivotal incident came on an air combat training mission in W-72, an exclusive block of airspace ten miles east of Virginia Beach: a pilot saw a dark gray cube inside a clear sphere, motionless against the wind at the entry point, and two jets only 100 feet apart were forced to take evasive action.

Graves says the squadron submitted a safety report that drew no official acknowledgement, with no further mechanism to report the sightings, and that he founded Americans for Safe Aerospace to support aircrew; by July 2023 he put its membership at nearly 5,000 and said it was working with more than 30 witnesses.

Gallaudet testified in writing that in January 2015 the operations officer of US Fleet Forces Command emailed all subordinate commanders under the subject "URGENT SAFETY OF FLIGHT ISSUE", attaching the GO FAST video, asking anyone who knew what the objects were to say so, reporting multiple near-midair collisions and warning that the exercise might have to be shut down.

Gallaudet, then commander of Naval Meteorology and Oceanography Command and a recipient, says the email vanished from his and other recipients' accounts the next day without explanation, and he concluded the information must have been classified in a special access programme run by an intelligence agency. At the same hearing Michael Shellenberger described an alleged parent programme consolidating UAP imagery.

The board pairs the two witnesses: Graves's unacknowledged squadron report and Gallaudet's recalled email describe the same failed safety machinery from opposite ends of the chain of command, and it sets the recall beside the range fouler reports, whose reporting stopped at Third Fleet.

How the videos reached the public, on the accounts the board carries: Mellon says he received them in the Pentagon parking lot from a Defense Department official, whom he has never identified, and gave them to the New York Times. TTSA then hosted and distributed the footage on its own platform, framing it as officially cleared.

The DD Form 1910 first reached the public through George Knapp with Elizondo's name and title redacted; the unredacted FOIA copy identifies him. On the board's reading, the August 2017 clearance and the October 2017 resignation were one planned exit sequence, which is inference from the dates and Mellon's account.

contested.text: AARO's case slides for the Senate Armed Services Committee on 19 November 2024 place the GO FAST object at about 13,000 feet moving around 45 mph with 60-knot winds, and say it did not demonstrate anomalous speeds or flight characteristics. The board notes that this addresses apparent speed only, not the safety email that Gallaudet says carried the same footage and was withdrawn the next day.
The same slides assess Aguadilla, GO FAST and Mount Etna but include no GIMBAL case.

The Navy's account and TTSA's conflict over how the videos were released: the clearance form expressly said not for publication, the Navy says there is no record of any request for unrestricted release, and the Department calls the 2007 and 2017 appearances unauthorised releases, while TTSA framed the footage as officially cleared.
On the board's reading, the April 2020 release was damage control rather than disclosure: it confirmed footage already in circulation and declined to characterise the objects.

The link to the carrier is weaker than the topic's title suggests: neither the Department's release statement nor Graves's testimony names the USS Theodore Roosevelt, and the board takes that association from other sources. AARO's slides also place GO FAST off Florida's east coast, not in Warning Area W-72 off Virginia Beach where Graves places the near-midair.

The Department of Defense says it has no record of the programme Shellenberger described, and former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick has denied it exists; on the board's reading a no-record answer is a records assertion rather than a denial that the programme exists.

lead.text: Ryan Graves testified that his Navy squadron, VFA-11, witnessed advanced unidentified objects on a regular basis in the airspace off Virginia Beach, including a near-midair in Warning Area W-72; two infrared videos from January 2015, GIMBAL and GO FAST, were released by the Department of Defense in April 2020 as still unidentified.

record.text: On 27 April 2020 the Department of Defense authorised release of three unclassified Navy videos, one from November 2004 and two from January 2015, which it said had circulated after unauthorised releases in 2007 and 2017. It stated that the phenomena in them remain characterised as unidentified, and that it was releasing them to clear up public misconceptions about whether the circulating footage was real.
GIMBAL and GO FAST are the two January 2015 videos in that release.
On 10 September 2019 Navy spokesman Joseph Gradisher stated that the Navy designates the objects in these videos as unidentified aerial phenomena.

A DD Form 1910 clearance request, released under FOIA, was submitted by Luis Elizondo as Director, National Programs Special Management Staff, OUSD(I), on 9 August 2017 and approved on 24 August 2017. It covers three .mpg files named GoFast, Gimbal and FLIR, and states their purpose as research and analysis only, not for publication, for a database to help defeat UAS threats.
Elizondo's resignation letter, released under FOIA, records his resignation effective 4 October 2017 with the same title.
In September 2019 the Navy stated that neither the cognizant Navy offices nor DOPSR have record of any correspondence responding to a request for unrestricted release of the videos in 2017.
TTSA's Form 1-K, filed with the SEC, names DeLonge, Semivan and Puthoff as directors, Elizondo as a significant employee, and Christopher Mellon on its advisory board.

The printed hearing records list Graves as a witness at the 26 July 2023 House Oversight hearing, as executive director of Americans for Safe Aerospace, and Gallaudet as a witness at the 13 November 2024 joint hearing.

The ODNI preliminary assessment reports that in 18 incidents observers described unusual movement patterns or flight characteristics, and says military sensors are not generally suited for identifying UAP.

summary.text: The account of the encounters rests on two witnesses who testified to Congress: Graves, a VFA-11 aviator, who described repeated sightings after a radar upgrade and a near-midair in W-72, and Tim Gallaudet, who described a January 2015 Fleet Forces Command safety email that carried the GO FAST video and was withdrawn the next day.

The videos have a documented paper trail of their own: an internal clearance form in August 2017 for research use only, public circulation that the Department later called unauthorised, a Navy designation of the objects as unidentified aerial phenomena in September 2019, and the Department's release on 27 April 2020.

Two disputes run through the topic: AARO's reanalysis of GO FAST, which finds no anomalous speed or flight characteristics but does not address the safety email that Gallaudet says carried the same footage and was withdrawn the next day, and the route by which the three files left the Pentagon.
